name: Rosa Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior designer at Meadowbank Creative, an agency of four in a converted barn just outside town. We do branding, labels and adverts for family firms and farm shops: a cider maker, a butcher, a garden centre, a dairy that sells ice cream. I use AI tools every day, for first drafts of labels, for photo clean-up, for writing the bits of copy nobody else wants to. Joan, who owns the place, says I'm the quickest she's had but I need to learn when to stop fiddling.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love driving out to a farm shop with Joan and seeing what the family's actually like before we design anything. Those are real people with real businesses. What wears me out is the evening emails, because farm families answer at nine at night after milking. My husband Ben's an accountant, and he jokes that we both live in spreadsheets now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are handy but nothing replaces knowing your customer. At church I'd say good, families can rest easy. Online I'd post a few before-and-after label designs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed, because I enjoy the tools. But it's good for us. Ben's job is safe, mine is safe, and I can keep building toward my own studio one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Meadowbank and keep using the tools. I'd ask Joan if I could take a couple of clients of my own, under her name, to learn the business side. Ben and I would keep overpaying the mortgage a little each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled and hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything else on your mind in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting a family, in a couple of years. We've got about nine months saved and the house, so we'd be all right. It's more about timing than money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the routine tasks AI takes over change your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It already has, honestly. Photo clean-up used to take me hours, and now it takes minutes. In this picture that just stays the same.

At **church** I'd say families can rest easy, and I'd post before-and-after labels.
think: I'm a little **disappointed**, since I enjoy the tools.
My husband's job and mine are **safe**, so I keep building toward **my own studio**.
do: Ask my boss to let me take **a couple of clients**.
S0.quote: Photo clean-up used to take me hours, and now it takes minutes.
fieldNote: She's already **AI-fluent** and slightly disappointed by a plateau.

**Family timing**, not money, is her main pressure.

steps.text: Ask Joan to let her run a couple of clients
Keep overpaying the mortgage each month with Ben
Use AI for label drafts and photo clean-up daily

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt, work hard, and look after your own. At church I'd say we should help families who struggle. Online I'd show how small firms can use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Ben is the one on my mind. His firm is already cutting junior accountants, and AI does bookkeeping well. I'm okay because I'm the AI person at Meadowbank, but my husband's bookkeeping work is exactly what goes first, and I'm more worried about him than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself Joan's AI lead, setting up quick label and advert workflows. I'd start a small side business selling branding packages to farm shops, mostly AI-made with my finishing touches. And Ben and I would push the baby plans back a year, until his job is clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My job looks fine, but Ben's could shrink or go. We'd still feel in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Ben feel about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's quiet about it, which isn't like him. He's started doing a course on financial advice, because he thinks people will still want a person for that. I think he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want the government to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with handouts. Help with apprenticeships, maybe, and tax breaks for small firms. Families and churches should do most of the carrying.

say: I'd say **adapt**, work hard and look after your own.
I'd urge church to **help families** and show small firms how to use the tools.
think: I'm more worried about **my husband** than me.
His **bookkeeping work** is exactly what AI takes first, and his firm is already cutting juniors.
do: Become the agency's **AI lead** with label workflows.
Start a **side business** selling branding packages to farm shops.
feel: **Anxious** about her husband's job, while still **in control**.

fieldNote: Her own job looks safe, but the **household** risk is her husband's.
She prefers **tax breaks and apprenticeships** to handouts.
She shifts **family plans** in response to his uncertainty.

steps.text: Set up AI label and advert workflows for Joan
Sell branding packages to farm shops on the side
Push baby plans back a year with Ben

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families need to pull together, and churches need to step up. I'd say people should help each other before waiting for government. Online I'd share what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we both lose our jobs by 2028. My design work, Ben's accounting, all thinking work. Being good with the AI tools doesn't help when the tools don't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd sell branding to every farm shop I can, while there's still a gap. I'd look at the hands-on side, like painting shop signs and building farm-shop displays, for the three years before robots. Ben and I would cut back hard and rent out the spare room. We'd put the baby on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake. Both of us at once is frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Neither of us does hands-on work, so it barely helps unless we switch. I could learn sign-painting, and Ben's dad is a builder, so Ben might work with him. Three years buys us time, not a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're okay for now, and that we might need help later. My dad would offer straight away. It would hurt my pride, but family is family.

say: I'd say families must **pull together** and churches **step up**.
People should **help each other** before waiting for government.
think: Being good with tools doesn't help when **the tools don't need** me.
do: Sell branding to **every farm shop** quickly.
Learn **sign-painting** and display building before robots.
**Rent out** the spare room and put the baby on hold.
feel: **Alarmed** and lying awake at **both jobs** going.
S2.quote: Being good with the AI tools doesn't help when the tools don't need me.
fieldNote: Her **AI fluency** gives no protection at full AGI.
**Both incomes** are thinking work, which drives the alarm.
**Family support** is her fallback, despite pride.

steps.text: Sell branding packages to as many farm shops as possible
Learn sign-painting and farm-shop display building

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to plan, so let's plan. I'd say apprenticeships for young people matter more than ever. At church I'd organise a jobs group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I can build my own studio and earn well before it hits. Ben can retrain into something more hands-on or people-facing. We'd still lose our jobs, but with savings and a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open my own small studio by 2028, using AI to do the work of three people. I'd save a third of everything I earn. Ben would start working with his dad's building firm part-time. We'd have a baby sooner rather than later, while we're still earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a baby a risk with incomes about to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But waiting doesn't make it safer. Better to have a baby now, while we're earning, than in 2032 with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after robots come around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then even building goes. I'd hope we'd have savings, the house paid down, and family around us. Beyond that, I don't know.

say: I'd say five years is **time to plan**.
I'd push **apprenticeships** and organise a **jobs group** at church.
think: I can build **my own studio** and earn well before it hits.
My husband can **retrain** into hands-on or people-facing work.
do: Open **my own studio** by 2028 using AI.
S3.quote: Better to have a baby now, while we're earning, than in 2032 with nothing.
fieldNote: She'd **bring family plans forward**, unlike the faster scenario.
She treats AI as a **force multiplier** for her own studio.
She'd organise a **church jobs group**, rooted in community.

steps.text: Open her own small design studio by 2028
Save a third of all earnings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, if people use it well. I'd say learn a trade, start a business, raise your family. At church I'd keep the jobs group going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do very well for most of the decade. My studio could grow, and Ben would have time to change. But by 2036 the design work still goes, and I'd be 37 with children to feed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open my studio in the next three years and grow it. I'd invest some profits in property, maybe a small rental. Ben would retrain fully into building with his dad. We'd have children in the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a little. It's a long way off, but it's still coming, and we'd have kids by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why property?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small rental is something real. I'd rather own bricks than shares, because people will always need somewhere to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest thing you'd want in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time with family. If I'm going to lose design work in ten years, I want to have built something for my children.

I'd say learn a trade, **start a business** and raise your family.
think: I'd **do very well** for most of the decade.
By 2036 I'd be 37 with **children to feed** and no design work.
do: Open and **grow my studio** within three years.
Have **children** while my husband retrains into building.
feel: **Anxious**, a little, because **kids** would be there by then.
S4.quote: I'd rather own bricks than shares, because people will always need somewhere to live.
fieldNote: She'd **build wealth** through property rather than markets.
Her plan blends **business, faith** and family, with her husband moving into his father's building trade.

steps.text: Open and grow her own design studio within three years
Invest studio profits in a small rental property

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Ben and I both lose our jobs at once. What would help is tax breaks for small firms, and apprenticeships so people like Ben can learn a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. If a couple are both in thinking work, the risk is twice as scary. People forget that.

headlineQuote: If a couple are both in thinking work, the risk is twice as scary.
portrait: Rosa is a **junior designer** at a four-person agency serving farm shops and family firms.
She uses **AI daily** and dreams of her **own studio**.
Her husband is an **accountant**, so household risk is high in fast scenarios.
She leans on **faith, family** and enterprise, not government handouts.
She swings from **calm** to alarmed and back to anxious with **a plan**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both she and her husband lose jobs at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Tax breaks** for small firms and **apprenticeships** for her husband.
